mandate_description:
The Community Health Tutor Programme at the University College Hospital (UCH), Ibadan is an agency school established within the Federal Training Centre for Teachers of Health Sciences to provide quality teacher-education for community health practitioners in Nigeria. The Programme operates under the supervision of the Federal Ministry of Health as part of the broader initiative to strengthen primary healthcare delivery systems across Nigeria.

The establishment of tutor programmes at UCH traces its origins to 1976, when the Federal Ministry of Health called upon UCH to assist in training tutors for Schools of Health Technology created across Nigeria to implement primary health care policies. The Federal Government recognized the critical shortage of qualified tutors to teach at these institutions and decided to establish an integrated training centre for teachers of health sciences at UCH, Ibadan.

The Community Health Officers' Training Programme commenced on October 15, 1979, initially under the Department of Public Health Nursing at the School of Hygiene, Eleyele, Ibadan. In November 1981, the Programme relocated to the University College Hospital campus. The Programme received full accreditation from the Community Health Practitioners Registration Board of Nigeria (CHPRBN) for four-year periods, confirming its compliance with national standards for training community health tutors.

The mandate of the Community Health Tutor Programme encompasses: training qualified community health practitioners to become competent tutors capable of teaching in Schools of Health Technology and related institutions across Nigeria; providing quality lifelong educational opportunities for Nigerian citizens registered and licensed by CHPRBN to practice in Nigeria; offering world-class training, research, and services for Primary Health Care Tutors in a conducive atmosphere renowned for quality and excellence; and contributing to the development of the primary healthcare workforce essential for achieving Nigeria's health goals.

The Programme admits candidates who are registered with the Community Health Practitioners Registration Board of Nigeria, possess current practicing licenses, and hold qualifications as Community Health Extension Workers or degrees in Community Health Science, Health Education, Public Health, or HND in Community Health. The teaching activities of the Programme are coordinated by the Institute of Education and the Community Medicine Department of the College of Medicine, University of Ibadan, with lecturers drawn from UCH and the University of Ibadan.

The Programme operates alongside other tutor training programmes within the Federal Training Centre for Teachers of Health Sciences at UCH, including the Environmental Health Officers' Tutors Programme, Nurse/Midwife/Public Health Nurse Tutors' Course, and Primary Health Care Tutors' Course. These programmes collectively address the need for qualified educators in Nigeria's health technology institutions.

The Computer Professionals (Registration Council of Nigeria), commonly known as CPN, was established by Decree No. 49 of 1993 (now CPN Act CAP C22 LFN 2004) as a body corporate with perpetual succession and common seal. The Decree was promulgated on June 10, 1993, and gazetted on August 9, 1993. CPN operates under the supervision of the Federal Ministry of Education, with the National Assembly performing oversight functions over its activities.

CPN was established in recognition of the increasing global prominence of Information Technology (IT) and its role as a driver of socio-economic development. The Federal Government identified the need to put appropriate regulatory mechanisms in place to ensure that growth and development in the IT sector occurs within an atmosphere devoid of quackery, arbitrary practice, and lack of standards.

The Council is charged with the regulation, control, and supervision of the computing profession and practice in Nigeria in line with Section 1(2) of the establishing Act. CPN's primary functions include: determining the standards of knowledge and skills to be attained by persons seeking to become members of the computing profession and improving those standards from time to time as circumstances may permit; securing the establishment and maintenance of a register of persons seeking to be registered under the Act to practice the computing profession; and publishing from time to time the list of such registered persons.

Additional functions of CPN include: determining academic and professional standards in Computer Science, Computer Engineering, Information Technology, and other related disciplines; accrediting institutions' courses and programmes as well as evaluating certificates in computing and related disciplines; regulating and controlling all persons and corporate organizations engaged or seeking to engage in the sale or use of computing facilities or the provision of professional services in computing; encouraging the education of computer scientists, engineers, and IT professionals in Nigeria; supporting and fostering research projects that advance IT and its applications; ensuring that computing profession ethics are upheld as stated in the society's code of practice and conduct; and defending and advancing registered members' interests.

Under the Act, it is mandatory for all persons and organizations seeking to engage, or already engaged, in IT training/education, sale and/or use of computing facilities, and the provision of professional services in computational or related machinery in Nigeria to be registered by the Council and licensed to carry out such activities. CPN maintains the power to apply administrative sanctions, including debarring any practitioner or organization that contravenes the Act. The Council has established a Centre of Excellence in Abuja and continues to intensify enforcement against illegal IT activities and quackery in the sector.

mda_name: 43. CONSULATE GENERAL OF NIGERIA, FRANKFURT, GERMANY
mandate_description:
The Consulate General of the Federal Republic of Nigeria in Frankfurt am Main is a Nigerian diplomatic mission in Germany established in 2013. It is the first and only Nigerian Consulate Office in Europe, reflecting the significant Nigerian diaspora population in the region. The Consulate is located at Weissfrauenstrasse 12, D-60311, Frankfurt am Main, Germany, and operates under the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The establishment of the Consulate General was necessitated by the large community of Nigerians residing within its consular jurisdiction. Nigerians constitute the largest sub-Saharan African group in Germany, with over 60,000 Nigerians estimated to be living in the country. Historically, the first Nigerians in Germany arrived on study visas with scholarships from the German government in support of Nigeria's post-independence development efforts. Many Nigerians are organized in professional groups such as Nigerian Scholars in Germany, Nigerian Medical Association, and umbrella associations like the Nigerians in Diaspora Organization in Germany and the Nigerian Community in Germany (formed in 1990 and incorporated in Bonn in 1992).

The Consular jurisdiction of the Nigeria Consulate in Frankfurt comprises five states in the South of Germany: Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Baden-Württemberg, the Free State of Bavaria, and North Rhine-Westphalia. Major cities within this jurisdiction include Düsseldorf, Heidelberg, Wiesbaden, Dortmund, Sindelfingen, and Mannheim, among others.

The mandate of the Consulate General encompasses providing consular services to Nigerian citizens and promoting bilateral relations between Nigeria and Germany. Specific services include: processing visa applications for foreign nationals seeking to visit Nigeria; passport application processing and renewal through online systems via the Nigerian Immigration Service website; issuance of Emergency Travel Certificates (ETC) to stranded Nigerians who lack proper immigration status to return home; citizenship services including age declaration, burial transit permits, change of profession, citizen identification and registration, and corporate registration; document legalization and authentication of documents issued in Nigeria; and providing help and assistance to Nigerians living within its area of jurisdiction.

The Consulate also provides emergency consular assistance including advice and support to victims of serious crime overseas and arranging for next-of-kin notification. In 2021, the Nigerian government launched a temporary passport to replace the Emergency Travel Certificate, with 30-day validity. The Consulate observes all public holidays within the consular jurisdiction areas as well as all national public holidays in Germany and Nigeria, including Christian and Muslim holidays. In addition to the Consulate General in Frankfurt, Nigeria maintains an Embassy in Berlin as its primary diplomatic mission in Germany.

mda_name: 44. COUNCIL FOR THE REGULATION OF ENGINEERING IN NIGERIA (COREN)
mandate_description:
The Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria (COREN), formerly known as the Council for the Registration of Engineers in Nigeria, is a statutory body established by the Federal Government of Nigeria with the mandate to regulate the practice of engineering in all aspects and ramifications. COREN was established by Decree 55 of 1970, amended by Decree 27 of 1992, codified as Engineers (Registration, etc.) Act CAP E11, 2004, and further amended by the Engineers (Registration, etc.) (Amendment) Act No. 3 of 2018.

The establishment of COREN empowered the Council to regulate and control the training and practice of engineering in Nigeria and to ensure and enforce the registration of all engineering personnel, including Engineers, Engineering Technologists, Engineering Technicians, and Engineering Craftsmen, as well as consulting and contracting firms wishing to practice or engage in engineering practice in Nigeria.

Under the establishing Act, COREN's primary functions include: determining who are engineers for the purposes of the Act; maintaining a register of engineering practitioners and issuing licenses to practice legally in Nigeria; regulating and controlling the practice of the engineering profession in all its aspects and ramifications; accrediting engineering programmes in universities, polytechnics, and technical colleges; and performing other functions conferred on the Council by the Act.

The Council is composed of members from the register of engineers, including: one person elected by the Council as President; six persons elected to represent the Nigerian Society of Engineers; four persons appointed to represent universities with faculties of engineering; one person appointed to represent polytechnics; one person to represent technical colleges; six persons appointed to represent the States of the Federation; four persons nominated by the Minister; and one person to represent each cadre of registered engineering technologists, engineering technicians, and engineering craftsmen.

COREN implements the Engineering Regulation and Monitoring (ERM) Programme established under the Engineers (Registration, etc.) (Amendment) Act No. 3, 2018, with objectives including: minimizing and eventually eliminating Nigeria's engineering and technological dependence on other countries through mandatory attachment of Nigerians to expatriate engineers on major projects; minimizing foreign exchange leakage resulting from foreign domination of engineering activities, particularly in petroleum and construction sectors; facilitating positioning of Nigerian engineering practitioners for global competition; ensuring that all foreign firms establish their design offices in Nigeria; and monitoring and enforcing compliance with the Engineers Registration Acts.

In 2023, COREN became a provisional signatory of the Washington Accord, an international agreement for the mutual recognition of engineering degree programmes. COREN operates under the supervision of the Federal Ministry of Power, Works and Housing and maintains regional offices across Nigeria, conducting professional examinations quarterly in various locations.

mda_name: 45. COUNCIL FOR THE REGULATION OF FREIGHT FORWARDING IN NIGERIA (CRFFN)
mandate_description:
The Council for the Regulation of Freight Forwarding in Nigeria (CRFFN) was established by Act No. 16 of 2007, which was enacted into law on April 30, 2007. The Council was formally inaugurated on August 18, 2008, and has been operational since then. CRFFN operates under the supervision of the Federal Ministry of Transportation as the principal regulatory body overseeing freight forwarding in Nigeria.

The Council is charged with regulating and controlling the practice of freight forwarding in Nigeria and promoting the highest standards of competence, practice, and conduct among practitioners. Under Section 30 of the establishing Act, a freight forwarder is defined as any person or company who arranges the carriage or movement of goods and associated formalities on behalf of an importer or exporter along the international boundaries of seaports, cargo airports, or land border stations.

Section 4 of Act No. 16 of 2007 establishes CRFFN's general duties, which include: regulating and controlling the practice of freight forwarding; determining the persons or classes of persons who constitute freight forwarders for the purposes of the Act; regulating and controlling all associations of freight forwarding agents; regulating and controlling persons engaged in freight forwarding; ensuring uniform standards of professional conduct and education relevant to freight forwarding practice; promoting the highest standard of competence, practice, and conduct among members of the profession; encouraging participation of members in international exchange programmes; and securing the establishment and maintenance of registers of persons entitled to practice as registered freight forwarders.

CRFFN is also mandated to determine the standards of knowledge and skill to be attained by persons seeking to be registered as freight forwarders in Nigeria and to raise those standards from time to time in accordance with international standards. The Council has obtained both national and international accreditation to run Higher National Diploma (HND) and Professional Diploma (PD) programmes for freight forwarders. The International Federation of Freight Forwarders Associations (FIATA) has accredited CRFFN to train and issue certificates in: Higher Diploma in Supply Chain Management and Professional Diploma in Freight Forwarding and Supply Chain Management. This accreditation is supported by the National Board for Technical Education (NBTE), which approved CRFFN to conduct FIATA Diploma programmes in Nigeria.

The Council's vision is to become Nigeria's leading transport player committed to the development of a modern, globally competitive freight forwarding system. CRFFN maintains offices in major port cities and is dedicated to achieving sustainable economic development through responsible transport initiatives in freight forwarding development and management. The Nigeria Customs Service Act, 2023 reinforces CRFFN's regulatory role over customs agents who operate within the freight forwarding value chain.

The Council of Legal Education was established under the Legal Education Act 1962, now re-enacted as the Legal Education (Consolidation, etc.) Act, Cap L10, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004. The Council is a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal, charged with responsibility for the legal education of persons seeking to become members of the legal profession in Nigeria.

The establishment of the Council traces back to the recommendations of the Unsworth Committee and the subsequent Denning Committee of 1960, which reviewed how training offered in the various Inns of Court satisfied the increasing needs of African countries. These committees recommended the establishment of a Council of Legal Education with the mandate to regulate legal education and practice in Nigeria. Following these recommendations, the Legal Education Act of 1962, the Legal Practitioners Act of 1962, and the Council of Legal Education Act of 1962 were enacted, leading to the establishment of the Nigerian Law School in 1962.

The Council's primary mandate is to have responsibility for the legal education of persons seeking to become members of the legal profession. The Council also has additional functions that were formerly the responsibility of the Nigerian Institute for Continuing Legal Education before the commencement of the consolidation Act. These additional functions include overseeing mandatory continuing legal education of legal practitioners in Nigeria (MCLE).

Under Section 3 of the Act, the Council issues qualifying certificates to persons stating that they are qualified to be called to the Bar. To be entitled to such a certificate, a person must have successfully completed a course of practical training in the Nigerian Law School, which includes time spent taking examinations at the end of the course. The Nigerian Law School, established under the Legal Education Act, provides professional certification to graduates of law from approved universities.

The Council's functions include: approving universities to establish law faculties and setting conditions for such approval; stipulating conditions that must be met by universities before they can be approved to establish law faculties, especially with reference to approved courses of study; conducting periodic assessment of law faculties to ensure compliance with its standards; prescribing good conduct as a condition precedent for admission to the Law School and for call to the Bar; granting various accreditation statuses to law faculties of universities; and introducing mandatory continuing legal education for legal practitioners.

The Council operates under the direction of the Attorney-General of the Federation, who may give the Council directions of a general character with regard to the exercise of its functions. All fees collected by the Council from students of the Nigerian Law School are paid into the Treasury of the Government of the Federation and form part of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. The Nigerian Law School currently operates seven campuses, one in each geopolitical region of the country, with the Nigerian Senate having approved the establishment of additional campuses.

mda_name: 47. COUNCIL OF NIGERIAN MINING ENGINEERS AND GEOSCIENTISTS (COMEG)
mandate_description:
The Council of Nigerian Mining Engineers and Geoscientists (COMEG) is the regulatory body for all professionals and firms in the Geosciences, Mining Engineering, and Metallurgy in Nigeria. COMEG was established through Act No. 40 of 1990 (now Act CAP C33 LFN, 2004) and was inaugurated on September 12, 2000. The President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria performed the inaugural Registration Ceremony of COMEG and presented the instruments of registration and practice to the Chairman of the Council on January 30, 2003. COMEG operates under the supervision of the Federal Ministry of Mines and Steel Development.

The struggle to establish a registration council for mining and geoscience professionals began in 1974, during a symposium on the "Role of the Nigerian Mining, Geological and Metallurgical Society in the Development of the Natural Resources of Nigeria." This symposium recommended the establishment of a regulating body, recognized in law, for scrutinizing the qualifications of and registering professionals in the field, similar to COREN for Engineers and the Medical Council for medical practitioners.

COMEG is charged with the responsibility of prescribing and enforcing the standards of education and experience for persons to practice as professionals in the Extractive Industries. The Council's major thrust is to regulate and control the practices of professionals in the fields of geology, geophysics, geochemistry, mining engineering, petroleum engineering, metallurgy, mineral processing engineering, and other related disciplines. These professionals, through their practices, contribute significantly to Nigeria's foreign exchange earnings, which largely sustain the economic activity of the country.

COMEG's regulatory responsibilities encompass: registering, regulating, and controlling the practices of Mining Engineering, Petroleum Engineering, Metallurgy, Mineral Processing Engineering, and the Geosciences in all aspects and ramifications; ensuring professionalism through education and regulation of practices in the Nigerian Extractive Industries; determining standards of knowledge and skill required for registration; maintaining registers of qualified professionals and firms; and ensuring adherence to professional standards and ethics.

The Council's vision is to be proactive in ensuring quality manpower for the Nigerian Extractive Industries while maintaining professionalism through registration, regulation, and training. COMEG has organized pre-accreditation workshops to develop Guidelines for Assessment Templates and has upgraded The Gem Magazine into a technical journal. The Council conducts periodic induction ceremonies to register new individual professionals and institutional members.

COMEG works closely with the Nigerian Mining and Geosciences Society (NMGS), which has statutory representation on the Council. Registration as a corporate member of NMGS is a prerequisite to registering with COMEG. The Council maintains the mandate that only COMEG-registered members should be employed in geosciences and mining engineering departments of tertiary institutions. COMEG has also concluded arrangements with partner organizations to conduct professional development training workshops on specialized topics such as the preparation of Bankable Mining Feasibility Study Reports.

Cross River National Park was formally established on October 1, 1991, through Federal Republic of Nigeria Decree No. 36, which simultaneously created the National Park Service to oversee the country's protected areas. The Park operates under Act 46 of 1999 (Cap 65 LFN 2004) as one of the seven national parks under the overall administration of the Nigeria National Park Service (NNPS), a Federal Parastatal under the supervision of the Federal Ministry of Environment.

The Park is situated in the southeastern corner of Nigeria in Cross River State, encompassing approximately 4,000 square kilometers of primarily moist tropical rainforest divided into two non-contiguous sectors: the larger Oban Division covering about 3,000 square kilometers and the Okwangwo Division spanning around 1,000 square kilometers (later adjusted to approximately 640 km² for Okwangwo and 920 km² for Oban). The establishment consolidated existing forest reserves into the park's two divisions: the Oban Division, originally gazetted as a forest reserve in 1988, and the Okwangwo Division, formed from three former reserves (Boshi, Okwangwo, and Nselle).

The park was first proposed in 1965, but serious planning did not start until 1988. The World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF-UK) played a leading role in planning and establishing the park, with a budget of $49.9 million. The Cross River gorilla (Gorilla gorilla diehli) was chosen as the park's theme animal, reflecting the park's critical importance as habitat for this critically endangered species.

Under the National Park Service Act, the park's mandate includes: establishment of an ecologically and geographically balanced network of protected areas under Federal Government jurisdiction and control; protection of endangered species of wild plants and animals and their habitats; conservation of wildlife throughout Nigeria so that the abundance and diversity of species are maintained at optimum levels commensurate with other forms of land use, ensuring continued existence of wildlife for sustainable utilization; preservation of outstanding scenic, natural, scientific, recreational, and other values; and protection and maintenance of crucial wetlands and water catchment areas.

Cross River National Park is recognized as a global biodiversity hotspot, hosting over 1,500 plant species (including 77 endemics in Oban), 119 mammal species, and 16 primate species. Key wildlife includes the endemic Cross River gorilla, Nigeria-Cameroon chimpanzee, drill monkey (Mandrillus leucophaeus), grey-cheeked mangabey, Preuss's guenon, and forest elephant. Over 900 bird species have been recorded, including the grey-necked rockfowl. The park is included in the UN's list of the 25 Biodiversity Hotspots in the World and is designated as an Important Bird and Biodiversity Area.

The park borders Korup National Park and Takamanda National Park in Cameroon, creating opportunities for transboundary conservation cooperation. An amending decree in 1999 converted the Nigerian National Park Service into a paramilitary outfit with increased enforcement powers. The Park is headed by a Conservator of Parks, with a Park Management Committee providing oversight. Management has established research stations and ranger patrol bases, with ongoing collaboration with organizations including the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) for conservation initiatives.

The Cross River Basin Development Authority (CRBDA) is one of the twelve River Basin Development Authorities established by the Federal Government of Nigeria to harness and develop water resources for agricultural production, water supply, and rural development. CRBDA was established under the River Basin Development Authorities Decrees No. 25 of June 15, 1976, and Decree No. 37 of August 3, 1976 (Niger Delta Basin Development Authority Decree). These decrees created eleven River Basin Development Authorities, including the Cross River Basin Development Authority. CRBDA operates under the River Basins Development Authorities Act, Cap R9, LFN, 2004.

The Authority was formally inaugurated on May 26, 1977, by the then Federal Commissioner of Water Resources, Alhaji Ibrahim El-Yakubu. Its jurisdiction initially included the whole of the then Anambra, Imo States, and part of Benue State. In 1979, following Decree No. 87 of September 28, 1979, the Cross River Basin Development Authority assumed its present geographical entity, covering the catchment areas drained by the Cross River and its tributaries. The Authority's current area of operation covers Cross River and Akwa Ibom States.

The CRBDA operates as a parastatal of the Federal Ministry of Water Resources with its headquarters located on Murtala Mohammed Highway, Calabar, Cross River State. The Authority is described as "a special purpose vehicle set out to intervene in food security and accelerate agricultural development through land and water resources management."

Under Section 4(1)(a)-(e) of the River Basins Development Authorities Act, Cap R9, LFN, 2004, CRBDA's statutory functions include: undertaking comprehensive development of both surface and underground water resources for multipurpose use, with particular emphasis on the provision of irrigation infrastructure and the control of floods and erosion, as well as watershed management; constructing, operating, and maintaining dams, dykes, polders, wells, boreholes, irrigation and drainage systems, and other works necessary for the achievement of the Authority's functions; supplying water from completed storage schemes to all users for a fee to be determined from time to time; handing over all lands to be cultivated under irrigation schemes to farmers; and developing and keeping up-to-date a comprehensive water resources master plan identifying all water resources requirements in the Authority's area of operation, through adequate collection and collation of water resources, water use, socio-economic and environmental data of the River Basin.

The Authority's management structure consists of a Chairman and seven other persons appointed by the President, including a representative of the Federal Ministry of Water Resources, all of whom possess detailed knowledge of the area of operation. CRBDA continues its mission of sustainable water management and agricultural development, aligning with federal mandates to promote all-season agriculture for socio-economic development and food security in the Cross River Basin region.

mda_name: 50. DAVID UMAHI FEDERAL UNIVERSITY OF HEALTH SCIENCES, UBURU, EBONYI STATE
mandate_description:
David Umahi Federal University of Health Sciences (DUFUHS), Uburu, Ebonyi State is a specialized federal university dedicated to health sciences education and training. The institution was originally established as King David Nweze Umahi University of Medical Sciences (KDUMS) by the administration of former Governor of Ebonyi State, Engr. David Nweze Umahi, FNSE, FNATE. The Federal Government of Nigeria subsequently took over the institution in 2022 as part of its policy to establish a University of Health Sciences in each geopolitical zone of the federation.

The take-over was formalized through a letter of notification dated September 15, 2022, from the Vice-Chancellor to the Executive Secretary of the National Universities Commission (NUC), Prof. Abubakar Adamu Rasheed. The documents included the Institution Take-Over Agreement between the Federal Government of Nigeria and the Government of Ebonyi State, as well as presidential approval for the take-over. In a response letter dated October 5, 2022, the NUC conveyed acceptance of the take-over and confirmed the renaming of the institution to David Umahi Federal University of Health Sciences (DUFUHS).

The Federal Government designated DUFUHS as the University of Health Sciences for the South East geopolitical zone of Nigeria. The Governing Council was constituted, and the relevant laws of the University were passed by the National Assembly of Nigeria in the first quarter of 2023. The institution is situated at Uburu in Ohaozara Local Government Area of Ebonyi State and operates alongside the David Umahi Federal University Teaching Hospital (DUFUTH).

The establishment of the University stems from a desire to enhance the quality of manpower development in the health sector and improve healthcare standards in Nigeria and the West African sub-region. The founding vision aimed to reverse medical tourism, which had led to significant capital flight from Nigeria to the UK, India, Saudi Arabia, and other advanced countries for medical treatment. The University's central goal is to develop critical competencies and expertise in the health sciences under the most conducive learning environment with the highest form of professionalism, ethics, and excellence.

DUFUHS has received approval from the National Universities Commission (NUC) to run seventeen (17) degree programmes in various faculties. Available programmes include: Applied Biology/Biotechnology, Computer Science, Industrial Chemistry, Industrial Mathematics, Industrial Physics, Microbiology/Parasitology, Biochemistry, Human Anatomy, Physiology, Biomedical Engineering, Dentistry, Medicine & Surgery, Human Nutrition/Dietetics, Medical Laboratory Science, Nursing Science, Pharmacy, Physiotherapy, Public Health, Optometry, and Radiography & Radiation Science.

The University operates with state-of-the-art facilities, including the David Umahi Federal University Teaching Hospital (DUFUTH), which is equipped with ultra-modern medical facilities, cutting-edge equipment, and innovative technology, including current modalities for medical imaging in the Radiology Department. Additional facilities include a Radiotherapy Centre, Ophthalmology Centre, Dialyzer Production Plant, Oxygen Production Plant, Virology & Quarantine Unit, and student hostels located within walking distance of the main campus. The University's motto is "Excellence, Scholarship and Productivity."

The Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF) was established under Section 11 of the National Health Act, 2014, as the principal funding vehicle for providing a Basic Minimum Package of Health Services to all Nigerians. The Fund serves as a catalytic financing mechanism designed to improve access to primary healthcare services, increase fiscal space for health, and strengthen Nigeria's national health system, particularly at the primary healthcare level.

The BHCPF is funded through multiple sources including: an annual grant from the Federal Government of Nigeria of not less than one percent (1%) of the Consolidated Revenue Fund; grants from international donor partners; and funds from the private sector and other sources. This funding structure was designed to ensure sustainable financing for healthcare delivery across Nigeria.

The Fund operates through four designated Gateways: The National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA) Gateway, which receives 45% of the Fund for strengthening primary healthcare facilities, providing essential drugs, vaccines, consumables, equipment maintenance, and human resource support; The National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) Gateway, which helps vulnerable and poor Nigerians access health insurance for the Basic Minimum Package of Health Services; The National Emergency Medical Treatment Committee (NEMTC) Gateway, which provides emergency ambulance services and urgent medical treatment; and The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) Gateway, which receives 2.5% for public health emergencies and outbreak response.

The BHCPF aims to achieve specific targets including: establishing at least 17,600 fully functional public or private primary healthcare facilities nationwide, with at least one in every political ward by 2027; ensuring at least one fully functional secondary healthcare facility per Local Government Area benefiting from the Fund in all states by 2027. The Fund specifically supports vulnerable groups including children under five years, the elderly, persons with disabilities, pregnant women, refugees, victims of human trafficking, internally displaced persons, and the indigent population.

The implementation structure involves coordination between federal, state, and local levels. State Primary Health Care Boards/Agencies and Local Government Health Authorities serve as conduits for fund disbursement and service delivery. The Fund represents Nigeria's commitment to Universal Health Coverage and symbolizes the nation's dedication to ensuring equitable access to quality healthcare for all citizens, regardless of their ability to pay.

Bayero University, Kano (BUK) was established by Federal Government Decree in 1975, with its legal framework formalized under the Bayero University Act (Decree No. 79 of 1979, as amended). The university traces its origins to Ahmadu Bello College, founded in January 1960 by the Northern Nigeria Ministry of Education to prepare secondary certificate holders for advanced studies in Arabic, Hausa, Islamic History, Islamic Studies, and English Literature.

Following the establishment of Ahmadu Bello University in Zaria in 1962, the college was renamed Abdullahi Bayero College, after Abdullahi Bayero, Emir of Kano. In 1975, it was elevated to Abdullahi Bayero University College with degree-awarding powers under continued ABU affiliation and its own Governing Council. By 1977, a Federal Government decree transformed it into an independent institution renamed Bayero University Kano, with Dr. Mahmud Tukur appointed as the pioneer Vice-Chancellor.

As a federal university, BUK operates under the governance structure established by Nigerian university legislation. The university is headed by a Chancellor appointed by the President, a Pro-Chancellor appointed by the President on the recommendation of the Minister, and a Vice-Chancellor who serves as the chief executive and academic officer. The Senate handles academic policy, curriculum approval, and examinations, while the Governing Council provides oversight for administrative and financial matters.

The university's mandate encompasses the advancement of learning through teaching, research, and community service. BUK is organized into multiple faculties including Arts and Islamic Studies, Agricultural Sciences, Computer Science and Information Technology, Communication, Engineering, Earth and Environmental Sciences, Education, Law, Management Sciences, Social Sciences, and Veterinary Medicine, along with two colleges: the College of Health Sciences and the College of Natural and Pharmaceutical Sciences.

The university maintains specialized research centers addressing regional challenges in agriculture, governance, public health, and education, including the Africa Centre of Excellence in Dryland Agriculture (ACE DA), the Centre for Advanced Medical Research, and the Centre for Infectious Diseases. The university library, established in 1964, supports teaching, learning, and research activities by acquiring, processing, preserving, and disseminating information resources. As the first university in Kano State and northwestern Nigeria, BUK has a unique mandate to serve as a center of excellence for cultural studies while advancing scientific and technological education in the region.

The Benin-Owena River Basin Development Authority (BORBDA) is one of the twelve River Basin Development Authorities established by the Federal Government of Nigeria under the River Basins Development Authorities Act of 1986 (which repealed the 1979 Act). BORBDA operates as a parastatal of the Federal Ministry of Water Resources with headquarters at Km 24, Benin/Sapele Road, Obayantor, Benin City, Edo State.

The Authority's operational area covers three states—Edo, Ondo, and Ekiti—and one senatorial district in Delta State. BORBDA is mandated to harness and develop water resources for sustainable agricultural production, water supply, flood control, and socio-economic development within the Benin-Owena River Basin.

Under Section 4(1) of the River Basin Development Authorities Act, BORBDA's statutory functions include: undertaking comprehensive development of both surface and underground water resources for multipurpose use, with particular emphasis on the provision of irrigation infrastructure and the control of floods and erosion, as well as watershed management; constructing, operating, and maintaining dams, dykes, polders, wells, boreholes, irrigation and drainage systems, and other works necessary for the achievement of the Authority's functions; handing over all lands to be cultivated under irrigation schemes to farmers after development; supplying water from completed storage schemes to all users for a fee; and developing and maintaining a comprehensive water resources master plan identifying all water resources requirements in the Authority's area of operation through adequate collection and collation of water resources, water use, socio-economic, and environmental data of the River Basin.

Key infrastructure projects under BORBDA include the Owena Multipurpose Dam, which provides irrigation water, hydroelectric power, and flood control; various irrigation schemes including the Ogbese and Eporo schemes aimed at boosting agricultural productivity; and urban and rural water supply schemes providing potable water to communities across its coverage area. The Authority aligns with federal government directives to promote all-season agriculture for socio-economic development, targeting youth employment through expanded irrigation infrastructure and related agricultural support services.

The National Board for Technology Incubation (NBTI) was established in 1992 by the Federal Government of Nigeria as a parastatal under the Federal Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology. The Board is the apex institution responsible for the coordination and management of the Technology Incubation Programme (TIP) in Nigeria, serving as the only agency of government mandated to commercialize research and development results.

NBTI's vision is to pursue the commercialization of technologies and technical innovations using Technology Incubation as a tool to enhance the attainment of technological, industrial, social, and economic competitiveness of the country and improve the quality of life of its citizens. The Board's mission is to develop the necessary infrastructure for nurturing technology start-ups, promote Nigeria's indigenous potentials through value-added and technology-related activities, and create an enabling environment for effective linkage amongst technology providers, entrepreneurs, capital, and know-how to accelerate the development of new enterprises.

The core mandates of NBTI include: creating, nurturing, and developing value-added technology-based enterprises; promoting and facilitating the application of indigenous technologies and knowledge; providing support services including training, business advice, funding, and technology knowledge to incubatees; linking graduating entrepreneurs with pertinent larger industries, the Nigerian Export Promotion Council (NEPC), and investors; and facilitating the establishment of Technology Incubation Centres (TICs) and Science and Technology Parks across the country.

NBTI has established a Technology Incubation Centre in each state of the Federation, with six extensions, totaling over 37 facilities nationwide. The first TIC was established at Agege, Lagos in 1993. The incubation process involves three stages: the first stage covers take-off and establishment requirements; the second stage marshals company growth including preparation of bankable investment plans, quality assurance, marketing strategies, and relocation to larger factory spaces. The programme supports entrepreneurs through both resident incubation (3-4 years maximum) and non-resident incubation (4-5 years) before graduation to the wider economy.

The Board operates through multiple departments including the Post Incubation and Extension Services Department, which monitors graduated entrepreneurs, provides benchmarking services, and supports the establishment of Industrial, Science and Technology Parks through Public-Private Partnerships. NBTI has successfully facilitated the listing of several incubatee companies on the Nigerian Stock Exchange, with some achieving local and international awards.

The Border Communities Development Agency (BCDA) was established by an Act of the National Assembly known as the Border Communities Development Agency Act, 2003 (as amended in 2006). The Agency is a federal government interventionist body created to ensure the sustainable social, economic, and infrastructural development of border communities in Nigeria. The formal inauguration of the Governing Board occurred on December 10, 2009.

BCDA operates under the Presidency with headquarters in the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja, and maintains offices in border states. The Agency addresses the persistent underdevelopment and neglect of border communities situated along Nigeria's international boundaries, which frequently lack adequate infrastructure, social services, and economic opportunities.

Under Section 3 of the Establishment Act, BCDA's functions include: preparing a comprehensive programme of action for the development of border communities; preparing and submitting proposals on projects for border communities to the President; advising the Federal Government on border areas development and related issues; consulting with relevant border communities and liaising with the Federal Government on areas required for overall development; identifying and determining infrastructural projects required for the overall development of border communities annually; executing border development policies, projects, and programmes; coordinating the activities of all relevant Ministries in implementing Federal Government policies and programmes for border community development; setting guidelines for the implementation and monitoring of Federal Government projects in border communities; planning and developing strategies for efficient and effective implementation of federal projects within border states; receiving and administering funds allocated from the Federation Account; and maintaining accounts with reputable banks.

The Agency covers over 2,000 border communities across 155 local government areas within 21 states that share international boundaries. Its intervention areas span both social and economic sectors: the social sector includes education, health facilities, clean water, and clean energy provision; the economic sector encompasses border markets, agricultural activities, grants, poverty alleviation, and empowerment programmes. BCDA serves as the secretariat of the Presidential Committee on the Security situation in Bakassi Peninsula, mandated to ensure the security and welfare of displaced persons from the ceded territory.

The Governing Board is chaired by the Vice-President of the Federation and includes the Attorney-General of the Federation, Ministers from various federal ministries, security chiefs, and representatives from the six geo-political zones, providing high-level coordination for border development initiatives.

The Budget Office of the Federation was established within the Federal Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning to provide budget functions, implement budget policies, and oversee fiscal policies of the Federal Government of Nigeria. The Office operates as the technical arm responsible for budget preparation, formulation, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation across federal government ministries, departments, and agencies.

The Budget Office derives its operational mandate from Section 81 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999, which stipulates that "the President shall cause to be prepared and laid before each House of the National Assembly at any time in each financial year estimates of the revenues and expenditure of the Federation for the next following financial year."

The mission of the Budget Office is to provide efficient and qualitative budget functions to Nigeria, geared towards promoting fiscal sustainability, transparency, and accountability in public finance management for national development in line with international best practices. Its vision is to be a world-class, technology-driven budget institution that serves as a catalyst for equitable mobilization and distribution of the nation's resources to engender sustainable socio-economic development.

All budget systems under the Office have three basic tasks: maintaining aggregate fiscal discipline, allocating resources in accordance with government priorities, and promoting the efficient delivery of services. The Office's specific functions include: revenue estimation using current and realistic assumptions on oil production and prices; estimation of non-oil receipts; developing macroeconomic frameworks used in aggregate fiscal estimates for the Medium Term Expenditure Framework; specifying fiscal policy objectives; analyzing macroeconomic frameworks and associated fiscal risks; coordinating the preparation of annual budget proposals; monitoring budget implementation across MDAs; and conducting budget evaluation and reporting.

The Budget Office is structured into six operational departments: Revenue/Fiscal Policy, Expenditure Social, Expenditure Economics, Budget Monitoring and Evaluation, Human Resources Management, and Finance and Accounts. Supporting units include ICT, Anti-Corruption and Transparency Unit (ACTU), Procurement, Legal, Stock Verification, Internal Audit, and SERVICOM. The Office of the Director-General coordinates overall budget functions and supports departments in achieving their mandates. Budget information is presented to facilitate policy analysis and promote accountability, with data reported on a gross basis distinguishing revenue, expenditure, and financing, classified by economic, functional, and administrative categories.

The Bureau of Public Enterprises (BPE) was established under the provisions of the Public Enterprises (Privatisation and Commercialisation) Act of 1999, which also created the National Council on Privatisation (NCP). The Bureau serves as the Secretariat of the NCP and is charged with the overall responsibility of implementing the Nigerian policy on privatisation and commercialisation.

The establishment of BPE has historical antecedents. The Technical Committee on Privatisation and Commercialisation (TCPC) was set up in 1988 under the Privatisation and Commercialisation Decree No. 25 to implement Nigeria's first phase of privatisation. Upon conclusion of its assignment in 1993, the Bureau of Public Enterprises Act of 1993 was promulgated, repealing the 1988 Act and establishing the Bureau. The 1999 Act further restructured the privatisation framework under the democratic dispensation.

The primary mandate of BPE is to drive the Federal Government's programme of privatising public enterprises, carrying out sector reforms, and liberalizing key economic sectors, especially the infrastructure sector. Under the Act, the Bureau's functions include: implementing the Nigerian policy on privatisation and commercialisation; preparing public enterprises approved for privatisation and/or commercialisation; carrying out public sector reform for maximum and efficient allocation of resources; facilitating the sale of shares of public enterprises through issuing houses in accordance with approved guidelines; engaging consultants, advisers, investment bankers, issuing houses, stockbrokers, solicitors, trustees, accountants, and other professionals required for privatisation purposes; and ensuring the overall success of the programme through effective post-transactional performance monitoring and evaluation.

The NCP, chaired by the Vice President, provides the overall strategic direction and policy framework, determining political, economic, and social objectives of privatisation and commercialisation. Some strategies utilized in the reform exercise include competitive asset sale, concession, core investor sale, guided liquidation, and private placement.

From 2000 to present, the NCP through BPE has successfully completed over 149 transactions and initiated far-reaching reforms in telecommunications, pensions, seaports, debt management, solid minerals, and the power sector—including the successful unbundling and privatisation of successor companies created from the Power Holding Company of Nigeria (PHCN). These reforms led to the establishment of regulatory agencies including the Nigerian Pension Commission (PenCom), Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC), Debt Management Office (DMO), Nigeria Electricity Liability Management Company (NELMCO), and Nigeria Electricity Bulk Trader (NBET).

The Bureau of Public Procurement (BPP) was established by the Public Procurement Act, 2007 (Act No. 14 of 2007), which came into force on June 4, 2007. The Act established both the National Council on Public Procurement and the Bureau of Public Procurement as the regulatory authorities responsible for the monitoring and oversight of public procurement in Nigeria.

The Bureau evolved from the Budget Monitoring and Price Intelligence Unit (BMPIU), also known as the "Due Process Office," established in 2001 as part of the Federal Government's anti-corruption and public expenditure reforms. The 2007 Act institutionalized these reforms by creating a permanent legal and regulatory framework for public procurement.

The primary objectives of the Bureau, as stated in Section 4 of the Act, are: establishing pricing standards and benchmarks; ensuring the application of fair, competitive, transparent, value-for-money standards and practices for the procurement of public goods, works, and services; attaining transparency, competitiveness, cost-effectiveness, and professionalism in the public sector procurement system; ensuring the accountability of public officers for public procurement decisions; and applying the provisions of the Act in preventing fraudulent and unfair procurement practices.

Under Section 5, the Bureau's functions include: formulating general policies and guidelines relating to public sector procurement for Council approval; publicizing and explaining the provisions of the Act; certifying federal procurement prior to contract award subject to thresholds set by the Council; supervising implementation of established procurement policies; monitoring prices of tendered items and maintaining a national database of standard prices; publishing details of major contracts in the procurement journal; maintaining paper and electronic editions of the procurement journal with archival systems; maintaining a national database of particulars, classification, and categorization of federal contractors and service providers; collating and archiving all federal procurement plans and information; undertaking procurement research and surveys; organizing training and development programmes for procurement professionals; periodically reviewing thresholds and procurement methods; and publishing annual reports on federal procurement.

The Bureau has the power to apply administrative sanctions, including debarring any supplier, contractor, or service provider that contravenes the Act. It provides the framework for procurement planning, methods, execution, enforcement, and review, ensuring that all procuring entities operate in strict adherence to the Act and regulations. The Bureau also maintains the database of accredited locally manufactured brands to promote local content in government procurement.

The Bureau of Public Service Reforms (BPSR) was established on February 4, 2004, by Presidential Directive during President Olusegun Obasanjo's administration as part of a broader initiative to revitalize the Nigerian Public Service. The establishment was formalized under Decree No. 25 of 1999, which outlined the Bureau's mandate and responsibilities. BPSR operates as an agency under the Presidency with headquarters at the Federal Secretariat Complex, Shehu Shagari Way, Garki, Abuja.

The Bureau was formed in response to growing inefficiencies within the Nigerian bureaucracy, including poor staff morale, low productivity, progressive decay observed during the oil boom era (1970s-1990s), and lack of proper incentives for public servants. Key initial goals included streamlining the public service, setting minimum standards for staff strength, and implementing remuneration reforms to attract and retain quality staff.

BPSR's primary mandate is to provide leadership in developing and implementing public service reforms to improve Nigeria. The Bureau's mission is to enhance the efficiency, effectiveness, and transparency of public service delivery through the initiation and implementation of innovative reforms and coordination among government agencies. Its vision is to facilitate the building of Nigeria's Public Service into a highly functional, professional, customer-focused, and results-oriented institution.

Key responsibilities include: initiating, coordinating, monitoring, and evaluating the implementation of reform programs and policies; conducting research on reform efforts and presenting best practice models for ministries, parastatals, and government agencies; provision of institutional capacity building for government agencies fostering continuous learning and professional development; improving service delivery through programmes like SERVICOM (Service Compact with All Nigerians), ensuring responsiveness and efficiency; delivering robust performance management systems to measure and manage performance of public servants and government agencies; providing workforce management solutions including recruitment, placement, and retention strategies; and delivering advisory services to government on public service matters.

The Bureau coordinates with the Office of the Head of Civil Service of the Federation, the Public Service Commission, and other government institutions involved in public service reforms. BPSR has developed guides on managing and reforming government agencies and parastatals, including web-based self-assessment tools. The Bureau leads the update of the National Strategy for Public Service Reform (NSPSR), a 10-year strategy built on four pillars: improving the governance and institutional environment, improving the socio-economic environment, improving public finance management, and improving civil service administration.

mda_name: 30. CENTRE FOR BLACK AND AFRICAN ARTS AND CIVILIZATION (CBAAC)
mandate_description:
The Centre for Black and African Arts and Civilization (CBAAC) was established by Decree No. 69 of 1979 following the successful and epoch-making hosting of the 2nd World Black and African Festival of Arts and Culture (FESTAC '77) in Lagos, Nigeria. CBAAC is a parastatal under the Federal Ministry of Information and National Orientation (formerly Federal Ministry of Arts, Culture, Tourism and the Creative Economy).

The Centre was created in fulfillment of Nigeria's pledge to keep the materials from FESTAC '77 in trust for the 59 Black and African countries and communities that participated in the festival. It houses all materials constituting the core collections, artifacts, and rare cultural items used during the historic festival.

Under Section 4 of the establishing Decree, CBAAC shall be a multi-disciplinary institution with responsibility for: the promotion of public interest in Black and African arts and civilization; the preservation of creative works of value from participating countries during FESTAC '77 or similar cultural manifestations; acquiring from zonal secretaries of the 1977 Festival and any other source, creative records relating to past and future world, regional, or national festivals of arts and culture relevant to Black and African arts and civilization; promoting understanding and appreciation of Black and African arts and cultures by involving the general public through lectures, discussions, symposia, exhibitions, performances, and demonstrations of arts and crafts.

The Centre maintains four main collection components: Archives, Library, Audio-Visual (housing FESTAC VCDs, CDs, DVDs, videocassettes, gramophone records, and promotional films), and Museum materials. The collections include materials on Nigeria and Africa's cultural festivals from 59 Black and African countries and communities.

In 2000, following the report of the Presidential Panel on the Review, Harmonization, and Rationalization of Federal Parastatals, Institutions, and Agencies, CBAAC was upgraded to a Pan-African Heritage Center, a status it maintains to date. The Centre's strategic mandate positions Nigeria as the arrowhead in the presentation, promotion, and propagation of African cultural heritage and civilization.

CBAAC achieves its goals through periodic seminars, workshops, public lectures, arts exhibitions, and symposia. The Centre maintains zonal offices across Nigeria and has hosted visits from prominent African leaders and international dignitaries. Its work emphasizes the contribution of Black and African peoples to world civilization and the preservation of Africa's rich cultural legacy for future generations.

The Centre for Management Development (CMD) is a national apex resource institution established in 1973 by the Federal Government of Nigeria as the operational arm of the Nigerian Council for Management Development (NCMD). The Centre received its legal status under Decree 51 of October 4, 1976, and operates under the supervision of the Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning.

The NCMD was established following recognition at a meeting of the National Manpower Board on October 20, 1965, that the major bottleneck in efforts to raise productivity was the comparatively low quality of management skills at all levels. The meeting noted that while considerable facilities for management training existed, lack of effective coordination and absence of a central information source led to wastage and unnecessary duplication of courses.

In 2004, CMD's mandate was enlarged when the Federal Executive Council, in line with the Federal Government's reform policy, approved the merger of CMD and the National Centre for Economic Management and Administration (NCEMA), Ibadan. Through this merger, CMD assumed additional responsibility to strengthen skills of public officers involved in economic planning, budgeting, project design, implementation and monitoring, and economic policy formulation.

The Centre's mandates, as established under the Nigerian Council for Management Development Act, 2022 (As amended), include: policy making, promotion, and coordination of managerial manpower development; accreditation and registration of management trainers and training institutions; advising on management policies; coordinating management training programs and developing standards; maintaining a register of training institutions; sanctioning or prohibiting unaccredited management trainers or institutions; and periodically assessing training programs offered by public and private institutions.

Under Section 16 of the establishing Decree, CMD's specific functions include: providing background information and technical data necessary for the Council's policy-making and coordinating functions; providing management advisory and consultancy services to Nigerian enterprises; establishing and maintaining an up-to-date library for management studies; publishing journals, research papers, and books on modern management and supervisory techniques; sponsoring, promoting, and conducting research into all aspects of management in relation to the Nigerian situation; and designing and providing suitable training packages for small-scale industrialists and officials of federal/state agencies responsible for developing small-scale industries.

CMD's vision is to be a world-class Management Development Institution that sets standards for excellence in management development and economic administration. The Centre operates from its headquarters in Abuja and maintains zonal offices in Kano, Lagos, Ibadan, Owerri, Gombe, and Uyo, enabling outreach to different parts of the country. CMD has facilitated the establishment of professional associations aimed at raising management standards in Nigeria.

Chad Basin National Park was established in 1991 under Decree No. 36 of 1991, which created the Nigeria National Park Service and designated five initial national parks. The park operates under Act 46 of 1999 (Cap 65 LFN 2004) as one of seven national parks under the overall administration of the Nigeria National Park Service (NNPS), a Federal Parastatal under the supervision of the Federal Ministry of Environment.

The park is located in the Sudano-Sahelian ecological zone of northeastern Nigeria, spanning Borno and Yobe States, with a total area of approximately 2,258 square kilometers. It is fragmented into three sectors: the Chingurmi-Duguma sector (1,228 km²) in Borno State within a Sudanian savanna ecological zone; the Bade-Nguru Wetlands sector (938 km²); and the Bulatura Oases sector (92 km²), both in Yobe State within the Sahel ecological zone.

Under the National Park Service Act, the park's mandate includes: establishment of an ecologically and geographically balanced network of protected areas under Federal Government jurisdiction and control; protection of endangered species of wild plants and animals and their habitats; conservation of wildlife throughout Nigeria so that the abundance and diversity of species are maintained at optimum levels commensurate with other forms of land use, ensuring continued existence of wildlife for sustainable utilization; preservation of outstanding scenic, natural, scientific, recreational, and other values; and protection and maintenance of crucial wetlands and water catchments.

Chad Basin National Park operates under Category II of the IUCN (International Union for Conservation of Nature), prioritizing conservation and sustainable tourism. The park combines the former Chingurmi-Dugoma Game Reserve, Gorgoram and Zurgun Baneri Forest Reserves, and Bulature Oasis. It lies within the historical region of the former Kanem-Bornu Empire.

The park is home to diverse wildlife including giraffes and ostriches (the only stronghold for these species in Nigeria), elephants, red-fronted gazelles, hippopotamuses, crocodiles, jackals, mongoose, spotted hyenas, and giant tortoises. Over 532 bird species have been recorded, including the vulnerable black-crowned crane, demoiselle cranes, white storks, and various waterfowl. The Bade-Nguru Wetlands (part of the internationally renowned Hadejia-Nguru Wetlands) and the Dagona Waterfowl Sanctuary are recognized as internationally significant habitats for waterbird populations and Palearctic migrants.

The park borders the Waza National Park in Cameroon, and authorities from both countries cooperate to prevent poaching and raise conservation awareness among local populations.

The Chad Basin Development Authority (CBDA) was established by Decree No. 32 of 1973 following the severe drought and famine in Northern Nigeria in 1972/73. The Federal Military Government created CBDA alongside the Sokoto-Rima River Basin Development Authority (Decree No. 33 of 1973) as the first River Basin Development Authorities in Nigeria. These decrees were subsequently amended by Decree 37 of 1976, consolidated by Decree 87 of 1979, and further revised by Decree No. 35 of 1987, which redefined CBDA as a water resources development agency.

CBDA operates as a parastatal of the Federal Ministry of Water Resources with its head office in Maiduguri, the capital of Borno State. The Authority's area of jurisdiction covers the whole of Borno and Yobe States and parts of northern Adamawa State, spanning from Maiha Local Government Area to Madagali Local Government Area (covering seven LGAs). Project offices are established in New Marte, Ngala, Baga, and Gora in Borno State; Potiskum and Gashua in Yobe State; and Michika in Adamawa State.

Under the River Basins Development Authorities Act, CBDA's statutory functions include: undertaking comprehensive development of both surface and underground water resources for multipurpose use, with particular emphasis on irrigation infrastructure provision and flood and erosion control, as well as watershed management; constructing, operating, and maintaining dams, dykes, polders, wells, boreholes, irrigation and drainage systems, and other works necessary for achieving the Authority's functions; handing over all lands developed under irrigation schemes to farmers; supplying water from completed storage schemes to all users for a fee; and developing and maintaining comprehensive water resources master plans identifying all requirements in the Authority's area of operation.

CBDA's flagship projects include the South Chad Irrigation Project, launched in 1974 to mitigate drought effects by developing 67,000 hectares of irrigable land in Borno State for enhanced agricultural productivity and food security. The Alau Dam, a multipurpose dam completed in 1988 with a capacity of 112 million cubic meters, irrigates 8,000 hectares in Jere Bowl, supplies water to Maiduguri, and supports tourism development.

Nigeria's membership in the Lake Chad Basin Commission (LCBC), established in 1964 by Chad, Cameroon, Niger, and Nigeria, provides a framework for transboundary cooperation in managing shared Lake Chad water resources. CBDA continues its mission of sustainable water management and agricultural development, aligning with federal mandates to prioritize all-season agriculture for socio-economic upliftment and youth employment in rural zones.

The Citizenship and Leadership Training Centre (CLTC) was established by the Citizenship and Leadership Training Centre Act to provide training for the development of citizenship and leadership for public benefit. The Centre is a parastatal in the Federal Ministry of Youth Development, principally serving as a human resource development outfit for training and molding Nigerian citizenry to become responsible and respectable citizens and leaders.

The Centre is unique as the only informal educational institution in Nigeria that executes experiential and Outward Bound education. It provides citizenship and leadership training in an atmosphere where self-discovery and self-actualization are based on individual competence and ability, irrespective of origin, belief, or class.

Under Section 2 of the Establishment Act, the objects of the Centre are to: provide training for development of citizenship and leadership for public benefit; enhance and expand individual awareness; inculcate in individuals qualities of self-discipline, self-reliance, and selfless service; develop national consciousness and international understanding; and seek to engineer a general reorientation of values.

The Centre's governance structure includes the Citizenship and Leadership Training Centre Management Board, a body corporate with perpetual succession and common seal, charged with general management and control of the Centre. The Board has powers to: establish Man O' War clubs and associations and formulate policy guidelines for running such clubs and associations; encourage and provide for research at the Centre; accept gifts, legacies, and donations consistent with Centre objectives; and with ministerial approval, manage property and investments.

CLTC operates training programmes across multiple categories: Man O' War Clubs and Commands for primary and junior secondary school students; training for senior secondary school students and teenagers; specialized programmes for civil servants (senior and middle-level public servants) to equip them with leadership qualities and citizenship responsibilities; and programmes for security agencies, paramilitary organizations, and corporate bodies.

The Centre's vision is to be a world-class provider of quality training that empowers Nigerians for good citizenship and responsible leadership. Its mission involves providing a sustainable framework for citizenship and leadership training and value re-orientation. The Mountain School at Shere Hills, Lamingo, Jos serves as the main training facility. The Centre operates through five geographical zones: Zone 1 (Northeast/North-Central with headquarters in Jos), Zone 2 (South-South/Southeast with headquarters in Port Harcourt), Zone 3 (Southwest with headquarters in Ibadan), Zone 4 (Northwest with headquarters in Sokoto), and Zone 5 (Lagos State).

mda_name: 35. CIVIL DEFENCE, CORRECTIONAL, FIRE AND IMMIGRATION SERVICES BOARD (CDCFIB)
mandate_description:
The Civil Defence, Correctional, Fire and Immigration Services Board (CDCFIB) was originally established as the Customs, Immigration and Prisons Services Board by Decree No. 14 of July 1986 under the Chairmanship of the Honourable Minister of Internal Affairs. The Board has undergone several name changes reflecting changes in its constituent services.

Initially, the Board was charged with administering the Customs and Excise Management Act (CEMA) of 1958, the Immigration Act of 1963, and the Prisons Act of 1972. In 1992, the Nigeria Customs Service was excised and placed under the Federal Ministry of Finance, changing the Board's name to "Immigration and Prisons Services Board" (IPB). With the enactment of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps Act in June 2003, which placed the administration of the new organization under the Board, its name changed to Civil Defence, Immigration and Prisons Service Board (CDIPB). Following the renaming of Nigerian Prisons Service to Nigerian Correctional Service and the inclusion of the Federal Fire Service, the Board became the Civil Defence, Correctional, Fire and Immigration Services Board (CDCFIB).

The Board operates under the Federal Ministry of Interior and is the governing body for four paramilitary agencies: the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), which focuses on protecting critical infrastructure, disaster management, crowd control, and internal security operations; the Nigeria Correctional Service (NCoS), responsible for inmate rehabilitation, prison security, and reformation programs; the Federal Fire Service (FFS), which handles fire prevention, control, investigation, and emergency rescue operations; and the Nigeria Immigration Service (NIS), which manages migration control, passport issuance, and border protection.

The Board's responsibilities include: recruitment and appointments into the four services; promotion and disciplinary matters affecting officers; manpower planning and training coordination; and policy formulation related to human resources in the paramilitary agencies. The Board has exclusive responsibility for the appointment, promotion, and discipline of all officers within these services.

CDCFIB's vision is to develop virile, motivated, and disciplined paramilitary services that ensure peace, safety, and stability of the country. The Board coordinates recruitment exercises for qualified Nigerians across all geopolitical zones in line with the Federal Character Principle, fostering inclusivity, unity, and equity in the composition of these essential security services.

The Cocoa Research Institute of Nigeria (CRIN) was established on December 1, 1964, in Ibadan, Oyo State, as a successor autonomous research organization to the Nigerian Substation of the defunct West African Cocoa Research Institute (WACRI). The establishment was pursuant to the Nigerian Research Institutes Act No. 33 of 1964. WACRI had been established in 1944 under Nigeria Statute Act No. 6 of 1950 with its headquarters at Tafo, Ghana, to conduct research on disease-free or disease-resistant cocoa production.

By virtue of the Nigerian Research Institutes Act No. 33 of 1964, CRIN's scope was expanded beyond that of WACRI to include research on kola and coffee in addition to cocoa. In 1975, the Agricultural Research Institutes (Establishments, etc.) Act further enlarged CRIN's research activities to include cashew and tea. In 2024, the Agricultural Research Council of Nigeria (ARCN) disclosed the inclusion of Vitex doniana (Black Plum) to CRIN's crops of coverage. Consequently, CRIN today has a mandate to conduct research on six crops—Cocoa, Kola, Coffee, Cashew, Tea, and Black Plum—throughout the country.

CRIN operates under the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development as a premier agricultural research institution. Its primary function is to conduct high-quality research and provide facilities for teaching and research with these agricultural products. The Institute maintains six substations located in the six geopolitical zones of Nigeria where mandate crops are cultivated in abundance.

According to the enabling legislation, CRIN's expressed objectives include: improvement of the genetic potential, agronomic and husbandry practices, including processing and storage of mandate crops; identification of the ecology and methods of control of pests and diseases affecting the crops; investigating effective utilization of crops and their by-products, and feasibility of small-scale production of such end-use products; integration of mandate crop cultivation into cropping systems where each crop is grown by farmers; and translation of research results and improved technologies into practice among farmers and manufacturers to improve production and socio-economic life of the people.

CRIN's vision is to be a centre of excellence of international repute in the research and development of its mandate crops. Major achievements include development of high-yielding and disease-resistant cocoa varieties, improved agronomic practices for sustainable farming, pest management solutions, and training of thousands of Nigerian farmers and extension workers in modern agricultural techniques. The Institute maintains skill acquisition sessions and extension workshops for stakeholders in the cocoa planting and processing industry.

The Code of Conduct Bureau (CCB) is established by Section 153(1) of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (as amended) as one of fourteen Federal Executive Bodies. The Bureau derives its powers, functions, and composition from Part I of the Fifth Schedule to the Constitution, and the Code of Conduct Bureau and Tribunal Act, Cap C15, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004.

The Bureau's historical antecedent traces to the recommendations of the Adegoroye Panel Report of 1975, which preceded the creation of the Public Complaints Commission and formed the basis for including the Code of Conduct provisions in the 1979 Constitution. The military administration of Murtala/Obasanjo inaugurated a Board before handing over power in 1979, though it could not make appreciable impact because the National Assembly of the Second Republic failed to pass the enabling law. The Bureau received its legal mandate under the Babangida regime in 1989, and the Code of Conduct provisions have maintained permanence in all subsequent constitutions (1989, 1993, 1995, 1999, and the current 1999 Constitution as amended).

Under Paragraph 3 of Part I of the Fifth Schedule, the Bureau's functions include: receiving declarations by public officers of their assets and liabilities; examining such declarations and ensuring compliance with requirements; retaining custody of all declarations and making them available for inspection by any citizen of Nigeria upon application to the Bureau; receiving complaints about non-compliance or breach of the Code of Conduct and referring cases requiring further investigation to the Code of Conduct Tribunal; and appointing, promoting, dismissing, and exercising disciplinary control over staff of the Bureau.

The Code of Conduct for Public Officers, contained in Part I of the Fifth Schedule, requires public officers to: maintain a high standard of morality and accountability; declare their assets (including those of spouses and unmarried children under 18) immediately after taking office and subsequently at the end of their tenure; not maintain foreign accounts except in the course of duty; not accept gifts or benefits beyond what is appropriate; and not operate any enterprise or business without Bureau approval, among other provisions.

The Bureau is headed by a Chairman and comprises at least nine members, all appointed by the President subject to Senate confirmation. The Chairman and members hold office for five-year terms and may be reappointed for one further term. The Bureau operates as a proactive anti-corruption agency working to prevent corruption through asset declaration monitoring and ensuring ethical conduct in public service.

The Code of Conduct Tribunal (CCT) is established by Section 153(1) of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (as amended) as one of the fourteen Federal Executive Bodies. The Tribunal derives its powers, functions, and composition from Part I of the Fifth Schedule to the Constitution and the Code of Conduct Bureau and Tribunal Act, Cap C15, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004.

The Tribunal serves as the adjudicatory body for matters relating to breaches of the Code of Conduct for Public Officers. It operates as a judicial body with specific jurisdiction to try and punish public officers who contravene the Code of Conduct provisions enshrined in the Constitution.

Under Paragraph 15 of Part I of the Fifth Schedule, the Tribunal consists of a Chairman and two other persons, all appointed by the President on the recommendation of the National Judicial Council.
